Here is what the evidence supports.",
  "key_points": [
    "Modifying daily nutrition by cutting dietary sodium and eating more potassium-rich whole foods often helps reduce arterial pressure.",
    "Aiming for 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly, alongside simple resistance work, supports healthy vessel flexibility.",
    "Prioritising 7 or more hours of restful sleep and practising slow breathing help calm the nervous system.",
    "Lifestyle shifts work alongside medical guidance and are not a replacement for clinical care when it is needed
Blood pressure simply reflects the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries as your heart pumps
It is recorded in two numbers: the top number (systolic) measures pressure during a heartbeat, and the bottom number (diastolic) measures pressure while the heart rests between beats
A single elevated reading is rarely a diagnosis on its own
Instead, it serves as a cue to observe your routines, track your numbers consistently, and discuss a plan with a healthcare provider
The most impactful change for many people involves reducing sodium intake
Most dietary sodium comes from pre-packaged, processed foods and restaurant meals rather than the salt shaker at the table
Health guidelines generally suggest aiming for less than 2,300 milligrams of sodium per day, or about 5 to 6 grams of total salt
\n\nEqually important is increasing potassium intake through whole foods, which helps your kidneys balance sodium levels and allows blood vessel walls to relax
You can build a heart-supportive plate by focusing on:\n\n* **Vegetables and leafy greens:** Spinach, broccoli, and sweet potatoes
\n* **Fruits:** Bananas, berries, oranges, and avocados
\n* **Whole grains and legumes:** Lentils, beans, oats, and brown rice
\n* **Lean proteins and healthy fats:** Fish, seeds, unsalted nuts, and olive oil
\n\nAdopting an eating pattern rich in whole foods, like the DASH dietary approach, often leads to noticeable improvements in blood pressure readings within a few weeks
You do not need intense athletic training to see benefits; consistency matters far more than intensity
\n\nHealth authorities recommend aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise each week
This can be broken into 30-minute sessions across five days, such as brisk walking, cycling, swimming, or yard work
\n\nIn addition to aerobic movement, research suggests that resistance and isometric exercises provide clear cardiovascular support
Simple bodyweight movements like wall sits, planks, or light resistance band sessions two to three times per week help improve vascular tone
If you have been inactive for a while, building up slowly allows your body to adapt comfortably
Chronic emotional strain, frequent poor sleep, and stimulant exposure can keep your system in a heightened state of alertness
\n\nSleeping fewer than seven hours a night on a regular basis is strongly associated with elevated blood pressure
\n\nDuring waking hours, deliberate breathing exercises can activate your body's relaxation pathways
Spending 10 to 15 minutes a day practising slow, paced breathing (aiming for fewer than 10 breaths per minute) has been shown to produce modest reductions in arterial tension
Reducing alcohol intake to recommended limits and avoiding tobacco products also remove immediate chemical stressors that elevate pressure
To get reliable data:\n\n* **Rest first:** Sit quietly with your feet flat on the floor and back supported for five minutes before measuring
\n* **Position correctly:** Use a validated upper-arm cuff rather than a wrist monitor, resting your arm on a table at heart level
\n* **Keep a log:** Take two readings one minute apart in the morning and two in the evening over a seven-day period, recording the average to share with your clinician

Seek medical evaluation under the following circumstances:\n\n* **Immediate emergency care:** If your blood pressure reading reaches 180 mmHg systolic or 120 mmHg diastolic, or if any elevated reading is accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, severe back pain, sudden weakness or numbness, changes in vision, or difficulty speaking
\n* **Routine clinical review:** If your home readings consistently average 140/90 mmHg or higher across several weeks despite making lifestyle changes
\n* **New or evolving symptoms:** If you experience frequent unexplained morning headaches, persistent dizziness, or episodes of feeling faint when standing
Brisk walking for 30 minutes on most days is one of the most thoroughly researched and effective forms of aerobic exercise for supporting lower blood pressure
